trigger: Asked for the shortest window that, if sorted, makes the whole array sorted.
key_idea: Find the first dip from the left and first rise from the right, then expand outward until every element outside the window is compatible with the window's min and max.
approach: Move low right while nums[low] <= nums[low+1]; return 0 if it reaches the end
Move high left while nums[high] >= nums[high-1]
Compute min and max of nums[low..high]
Expand low left while nums[low-1] > window min
Expand high right while nums[high+1] < window max
Return high - low + 1
gotcha: Forgetting the expansion step: elements outside the initial dip may still be larger than the window's min, e.g. [1,3,2,2,2].

trigger: Two trees must be overlaid node by node, combining values where both exist.
key_idea: Recurse on both trees in lockstep; if one side is null just return the other subtree, otherwise build a node with the summed value.
approach: If root1 is None return root2; if root2 is None return root1
Create node with root1.val + root2.val
Set node.left = merge(root1.left, root2.left)
Set node.right = merge(root1.right, root2.right)
Return node
gotcha: Recursing into a null node's children raises an error; the base case must return the non-null subtree immediately.

trigger: Rearrange characters so identical ones are at least k positions apart.
key_idea: Always place the most frequent available character, then park it in a cooldown queue of size k so it cannot be reused until k other placements happen.
approach: Count characters; push (-count, char) into a max-heap
Pop the most frequent char, append it to the result
Push (remaining count, char) onto a deque
When deque reaches size k, pop its front and re-push to heap if count > 0
Return result if its length equals len(s), else empty string
gotcha: k == 0 means no constraint and must return s directly; also the result is invalid if the heap empties before all characters are placed.

trigger: Same tasks need a cooldown of n intervals between them and you want minimum total time.
key_idea: Greedily schedule the most frequent remaining tasks in each cycle of n+1 slots; leftover slots become idle. The closed form is max(len(tasks), (maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countOfMaxFreq).
approach: Count task frequencies; push (-count, task) into a max-heap
Repeat while heap non-empty: run a cycle of n+1 slots
In each slot pop the most frequent task, decrement, stash it if count remains
If heap empty but stashed tasks remain, count an idle slot
After the cycle push stashed tasks back
Return total slots used
gotcha: Idle slots must not be counted after the last real task finishes; the learner's code only adds '#' when tasks are still pending.

trigger: Maximum product of three numbers from an array that may contain negatives.
key_idea: The answer is either the three largest numbers or the two most negative numbers times the largest, because two negatives multiply to a positive.
approach: Sort the array
Compute product of the last three elements
Compute product of first two elements and the last element
Return the max of the two

complexity.space: O(1) extra (or O(n) for O(n) min/max tracking)

gotcha: Forgetting the two-smallest-negatives case, e.g. [-10,-10,1,3,2] has answer 300 not 6.

trigger: Find the smallest range that touches at least one element from each of k sorted lists.
key_idea: Keep one element from every list in a min-heap; the range is [heap min, running max]; advancing the minimum's list is the only way to shrink the range.
approach: Push the first element of each list as (value, listIndex, position) into a min-heap
Track the max of those first elements
Pop the min; if its list is exhausted stop
Push the next element from that list, update max
If newMax - heapMin beats best range, update the answer
Return the best range

complexity.time: O(N log k) where N is total elements

gotcha: Stop as soon as any list runs out; once a list is exhausted no further range can include all k lists.

trigger: Per-level statistics of a binary tree (average, max, count per level).
key_idea: Level-order BFS with a snapshot of the queue size lets you process exactly one level per outer loop iteration.
approach: Push root into a deque
While deque not empty, record levelSize = len(queue)
Pop levelSize nodes, summing values and enqueuing children
Append levelSum / levelSize to the result
Return the result list
gotcha: Use float division and sum as float; integer division would silently truncate averages.

trigger: Best value over every contiguous subarray of a fixed length k.
key_idea: A fixed-size window sum can be updated in O(1) by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one; maximizing the sum maximizes the average.
approach: Sum the first k elements as the initial window
For i from k to n-1, add nums[i] and subtract nums[i-k]
Track the maximum window sum seen
Return max sum divided by k
gotcha: Dividing inside the loop wastes precision and time; compare sums and divide only once at the end.

trigger: Array holds numbers 1..n with one duplicated and one missing.
key_idea: Because values are in 1..n, each value has a home index value-1; swap elements into their homes and the one index whose value is wrong reveals both the duplicate and the missing number.
approach: Iterate i; let j = nums[i] - 1
If nums[i] != nums[j], swap them and stay at i
Otherwise advance i
Scan again: the first i where nums[i] != i+1 gives [nums[i], i+1]
gotcha: Compare nums[i] with nums[j], not i with j; otherwise a duplicate causes an infinite swap loop.

trigger: Choose the maximum number of pairs where each next pair starts after the previous one ends.
key_idea: This is the classic non-overlapping-intervals problem: sort by end value and greedily take every pair that starts after the current chain end.
approach: Sort pairs by their right endpoint
Initialize currEnd = -infinity and count = 0
For each pair, if left > currEnd, take it and set currEnd = right
Return count

complexity.space: O(n) for the sorted copy (or O(1) if sorted in place)

gotcha: Sorting by start instead of end breaks the greedy; a long early-starting pair could block many short ones.

trigger: Count all palindromic substrings of a string.
key_idea: Every palindrome has a center; expand outward from each of the 2n-1 centers (single char and between chars) while the ends match. The learner used memoized recursion on (l, r), which is O(n^2) states but heavier.
approach: For each index i, treat it as an odd-length center
Expand l, r outward while s[l] == s[r], counting each match
Repeat with center between i and i+1 for even lengths
Sum the counts from all centers
gotcha: Missing the even-length centers halves the answer; 'aa' has 3 palindromic substrings, not 2.

trigger: Build a tree where the root is the max element and subtrees come from the left and right slices.
key_idea: The definition is already recursive: find the max in the range, make it the root, recurse on the two halves around it.
approach: Define construct(l, r) on the half-open range [l, r)
Return None if the range is empty
Find the index of the max in the range
Root = that value; root.left = construct(l, maxIdx); root.right = construct(maxIdx+1, r)
Call construct(0, n)

complexity.time: O(n^2) worst case, O(n log n) average

gotcha: Off-by-one in the range bounds; using a half-open [l, r) makes the empty check simply l == r.

trigger: Sorted array, return the k elements closest to a value x, in sorted order.
key_idea: The answer is a contiguous window of length k; binary search over its left boundary in [0, n-k] by comparing the distances of arr[mid] and arr[mid+k] to x.
approach: Set left = 0, right = n - k
While left < right, mid = (left + right) // 2
If x - arr[mid] > arr[mid+k] - x, the window should shift right: left = mid + 1
Otherwise right = mid
Return arr[left : left+k]
gotcha: Compare raw differences, not absolute values; abs() breaks the tie-breaking rule that prefers the smaller element.

trigger: Width of a level counts the null gaps between the leftmost and rightmost nodes.
key_idea: Number nodes as if in a complete binary tree (left child 2i, right child 2i+1); the width of a level is last index minus first index plus one.
approach: BFS with (node, index) pairs, starting at (root, 0)
For each level, width = lastIndex - firstIndex + 1
Enqueue children with indices 2*i and 2*i+1
Track the maximum width across levels
gotcha: Indices grow exponentially with depth; in Python this is fine, but in other languages normalize by subtracting the level's first index.

trigger: Palindrome check with permission to delete at most one character.
key_idea: Walk inward from both ends; at the first mismatch you have exactly two options, skip the left char or skip the right char, and one of them must then be a plain palindrome.
approach: Set l = 0, r = len(s) - 1
While s[l] == s[r], move both inward
On mismatch, return isPalindrome(l+1, r) or isPalindrome(l, r-1)
If loop finishes, return True
gotcha: Only one deletion is allowed, so the helper must be a strict palindrome check with no further skipping.

trigger: Undirected graph that is a tree plus exactly one extra edge; find the edge to remove.
key_idea: Add edges one by one to a Union-Find; the first edge whose endpoints are already connected closes a cycle and is the answer.
approach: Initialize parent and rank arrays for nodes 1..n
For each edge (a, b), find roots of a and b
If roots are equal, return [a, b]
Otherwise union them by rank
gotcha: Nodes are 1-indexed, so allocate n+1 slots; also return the last such edge in input order, which the first-cycle check guarantees.

trigger: Top k most frequent items with a tie-break on lexicographic order.
key_idea: Count frequencies, then order by (-count, word) so the heap or sort handles both the frequency and the alphabetical tie-break. The learner's variant buckets by count and uses a per-bucket trie to emit words alphabetically.
approach: Count words with a Counter
Push (-count, word) tuples into a heap
Pop k times to collect the answer
Return the collected words

complexity.time: O(n log n) for heap; O(n + k) with bucket + trie

gotcha: Negating the count but not the word makes the tuple order correct; negating both is impossible for strings, so be careful with min-heap direction.

trigger: Count the size of connected components of 1s in a grid.
key_idea: Flood-fill each unvisited land cell, marking cells as water when visited so each cell is counted once; the answer is the largest fill size.
approach: Scan every cell; on a 1, start a BFS/DFS
Mark the cell 0 when enqueued to avoid revisits
Expand to 4-directional neighbors that are in bounds and equal to 1
Count cells in the fill and track the maximum
Return the maximum (0 if no land)

complexity.space: O(m*n) worst case queue or recursion

gotcha: Mark a cell visited when you enqueue it, not when you pop it, or the same cell gets counted multiple times.

trigger: Sorted data with unknown length accessed through a get(i) that returns a sentinel past the end.
key_idea: Exponential search: double the high index until reader.get(high) >= target, then run normal binary search inside [0, high].
approach: Start with low = 0, high = 1
While reader.get(high) < target, double high
Binary search between low and high
Return the index of target or -1
gotcha: The out-of-bounds sentinel is 2^31 - 1 which is larger than any valid value, so the doubling loop naturally stops.

trigger: Maintain the kth largest value as numbers keep arriving.
key_idea: Keep a min-heap of the k largest elements seen; its root is always the kth largest, and anything smaller than the root can be discarded.
approach: Store k and an empty min-heap
On add, push the value
If heap size exceeds k, pop the smallest
Return heap[0]
gotcha: Initial nums may contain fewer than k elements; pushing through add handles it and the heap fills up as values arrive.

trigger: Sorted array and an O(log n) requirement for locating a target.
key_idea: Halve the search range each step by comparing the middle element with the target.
approach: Set start = 0, end = n - 1
While start <= end, mid = (start + end) // 2
If nums[mid] == target return mid
If nums[mid] > target, end = mid - 1; else start = mid + 1
Return -1
gotcha: Using end = mid or start = mid without +-1 causes an infinite loop on a two-element range.

trigger: Count contiguous subarrays whose product (of positive numbers) stays below k.
key_idea: With positives, the product grows monotonically as the window expands, so every valid window ending at r contributes r - l + 1 subarrays.
approach: Return 0 if k <= 1
For each r, multiply nums[r] into the running product
While product >= k, divide out nums[l] and advance l
Add r - l + 1 to the count
Return the count
gotcha: k <= 1 must be handled up front; otherwise the shrink loop can push l past r and index errors follow.

trigger: Repeatedly add bookings and reject any that overlap existing ones.
key_idea: Keep the intervals sorted; a new [s, e) is valid only if the previous interval ends by s and the next interval starts at or after e.
approach: Keep a sorted list of (start, end) tuples
Find insertion index with bisect_right
Reject if previous interval's end > start
Reject if next interval's start < end
Otherwise insert and return True

complexity.time: O(log n) search plus O(n) insert per booking

gotcha: Intervals are half-open, so an event ending at 20 and another starting at 20 do not overlap.

trigger: For each element, how far to the next greater element on the right.
key_idea: Maintain a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures; when a warmer day arrives, it resolves every colder day still on the stack.
approach: Initialize res with zeros and an empty stack of indices
For each day i, while top of stack is colder than temps[i], pop it
Set res[popped] = i - popped
Push i
Return res
gotcha: Push indices rather than temperatures, or you cannot compute the distance.

trigger: Next greater element for a subset of values, looked up in a larger array.
key_idea: Precompute next-greater for every element of nums2 with a decreasing stack, store it in a map, then answer nums1 queries by lookup.
approach: Iterate nums2 with a stack of values
While top < current, pop and record map[popped] = current
Push current
Return [map.get(n, -1) for n in nums1]
gotcha: Elements left on the stack have no greater element; default the lookup to -1 instead of inserting them.

trigger: Reach the top taking 1 or 2 steps, paying a cost per step, with a free start at index 0 or 1.
key_idea: dp[i] is the min cost to stand on step i; you arrive from i-1 or i-2 and pay the cost of the step you left.
approach: Set dp[0] = dp[1] = 0
For i from 2 to n, dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2])
Return dp[n]
gotcha: The top is index n, one past the last step, so dp has n+1 entries and you pay for the step you leave, not the one you land on.

trigger: Find gaps common to every employee's schedule of sorted, non-overlapping intervals.
key_idea: Flatten all intervals, sort by start, and sweep merging overlaps; each time the next interval starts after the merged end, that gap is free time for everyone.
approach: Flatten all employees' intervals into one list
Sort by start
Keep prev as the current merged interval
If prev.end < next.start, record gap (prev.end, next.start) and set prev = next
Else extend prev.end = max(prev.end, next.end)
Return the gaps

complexity.time: O(N log N) for N total intervals

gotcha: Extend prev.end with max, not just assignment, since a later interval may end earlier than the current merged block.

trigger: Rearrange characters so no two adjacent characters are equal.
key_idea: It is possible iff the most frequent char count is at most (n+1)//2; place that char at even indices first, then fill remaining chars into the leftover even slots and then odd slots.
approach: Count characters and find the most frequent one
Return empty string if its count > (n+1)//2
Fill the most frequent char at indices 0, 2, 4, ...
Continue placing other chars at the next even indices, wrapping to index 1
Join and return the array
gotcha: The most frequent character must be placed first; placing others first can leave adjacent even slots for it.

trigger: Count how many characters of one string belong to a set defined by another string.
key_idea: Put the jewel characters in a set for O(1) membership and count stone characters that are members.
approach: Build a set from jewels
Iterate stones and count characters found in the set
Return the count
gotcha: Letters are case sensitive; do not lowercase either string.

trigger: Minimum difference between any two values in a BST.
key_idea: In-order traversal visits BST values in sorted order, so the minimum difference is always between consecutive visited nodes.
approach: Do an in-order traversal keeping prev node
At each node, update diff = min(diff, node.val - prev.val)
Set prev = node
Return diff
gotcha: Checking 'if self.prev' fails when the previous node's value is 0; check 'is not None' instead.

trigger: Can the nodes be split into two groups so every edge crosses between groups (2-coloring).
key_idea: All neighbors of a node must be in the same group, so union every node's neighbors together; if a node ever shares a root with one of its neighbors, it is not bipartite. BFS 2-coloring is the equivalent alternative.
approach: Initialize Union-Find over n nodes
For each node, take its first neighbor as the group anchor
For every neighbor, if find(node) == find(neighbor) return False
Union the neighbor with the anchor
Return True
gotcha: Graph may be disconnected; iterate over every node, not just a BFS from node 0.

trigger: Directed graph; nodes are safe if every path from them reaches a terminal node (no cycle reachable).
key_idea: DFS with a memo: mark a node unsafe on entry (in progress), then safe only after all neighbors prove safe; revisiting an in-progress node means a cycle.
approach: Keep a dict safe[node] initially empty
On visiting a node, set safe[node] = False before recursing
Recurse on neighbors; if any is unsafe return False
Set safe[node] = True and return True
Collect nodes where dfs returns True
gotcha: Marking a node False before exploring its neighbors is what detects cycles; setting it only after would loop forever.

trigger: Minimum number of buses (transfers) to get from a source stop to a target stop.
key_idea: BFS over buses rather than stops: two buses are adjacent if they share a stop, so each BFS layer costs one more bus.
approach: Map each stop to the list of buses serving it
Start BFS with all buses at the source stop, count = 1
For each bus in the layer, scan its stops; if target found return count
Enqueue unseen buses at each stop
Increment count per layer; return -1 if BFS ends

complexity.time: O(sum of route lengths * buses per stop)

gotcha: source == target must return 0 before any BFS; also mark buses seen on enqueue to avoid re-expanding.

trigger: Minimum number of buses (transfers) to get from a source stop to a target stop.
key_idea: BFS over buses with a stop-to-buses map; also track visited stops so each stop is scanned only once, which keeps the traversal linear in total route size.
approach: Build stop -> buses map; return -1 if source or target is unknown
Start with all buses at source as the first layer, count = 1
For each bus, iterate its stops that are not yet visited
Return count if a stop equals target; otherwise enqueue unseen buses
Increment count per layer; return -1 at the end
gotcha: Without a visited-stops set, a hub stop shared by many routes is rescanned per bus and can time out.

trigger: Compare two strings where '#' means backspace, ideally in O(1) space.
key_idea: Scan both strings from the end; count pending backspaces to skip deleted characters, then compare the next surviving characters.
approach: Start pointers at the ends of s and t
For each string, skip back over chars while tracking backspace count
If both pointers are exhausted return True; if only one, return False
Compare the surviving characters; mismatch returns False
Move both pointers left and repeat
gotcha: A backspace can only cancel characters before it, which is why you must scan right to left, not left to right.

trigger: Array rises then falls; find the peak in O(log n).
key_idea: Compare mid with mid+1: if arr[mid] < arr[mid+1] you are on the ascending slope so the peak is right, otherwise it is at mid or left.
approach: Set low = 0, high = n - 1
While low < high, mid = (low + high) // 2
If arr[mid] > arr[mid+1], high = mid
Else low = mid + 1
Return low
gotcha: Use low < high with high = mid (not mid - 1) so the peak itself is never skipped.

trigger: Execute a list of turn/move commands on a grid with obstacles and report the farthest point.
key_idea: Store obstacles in a set of tuples and step one unit at a time, stopping a move early when the next cell is blocked; track max x^2 + y^2 along the way.
approach: Put obstacle coordinates into a set
Keep a direction index over (dx, dy) for N, E, S, W
On -1 or -2, rotate the direction index
On k, step up to k times, breaking if the next cell is an obstacle
Update max distance squared after every step
gotcha: The answer is the maximum distance ever reached, not the final position; update inside the step loop.

trigger: Walk a clockwise spiral from a start cell, recording only cells that fall inside the grid.
key_idea: Spiral step lengths follow 1,1,2,2,3,3,...: every two direction changes the run length grows by one; keep walking outside the grid and just skip out-of-bounds cells.
approach: Directions in clockwise order: east, south, west, north
Loop until rows*cols cells collected
For two consecutive directions, walk 'width' steps each
Record a cell only if it lies inside the grid
After the two runs, increase width by one
gotcha: The starting cell must be recorded before the first move; append inside the step loop before incrementing coordinates.

trigger: Pop the most frequent element, breaking ties by most recently pushed.
key_idea: Keep a stack per frequency level: pushing val appends it to stack[freq[val]]; popping takes from the highest-frequency stack, which automatically respects recency.
approach: Maintain freq map, group map from frequency to list, and maxFreq
On push, increment freq[val], update maxFreq, append val to group[freq[val]]
On pop, pop from group[maxFreq], decrement freq[x]
If group[maxFreq] becomes empty, decrement maxFreq
Return x
gotcha: A value with frequency 3 appears in group[1], group[2] and group[3]; do not remove it from lower groups on pop.

trigger: Longest contiguous subarray containing at most two distinct values.
key_idea: Grow a window with a frequency map; whenever the map exceeds two keys, shrink from the left until it has two again.
approach: Keep a count map and left pointer l
For each r, add fruits[r] to the map
While map has more than 2 keys, decrement fruits[l], delete at zero, advance l
Update the best length r - l + 1
Return the best
gotcha: Delete keys whose count hits zero, otherwise len(map) never shrinks and the window never becomes valid.

trigger: Sum of the minimum over every subarray (contribution counting).
key_idea: Each element is the minimum of (index - prevSmaller) * (nextSmaller - index) subarrays; a monotonic increasing stack finds both boundaries in one pass.
approach: Append a sentinel 0 to flush the stack at the end
Iterate i; while arr[stack top] > arr[i], pop index
left = index - (new stack top or -1); right = i - index
Add arr[index] * left * right to the result
Push i; return result modulo 10^9 + 7
gotcha: Handle duplicates with strict inequality on one side only; popping on > (not >=) avoids double-counting equal values.

trigger: Minimum insertions to balance a parentheses string.
key_idea: A counter of unmatched '(' replaces a stack; a ')' with no open partner needs an inserted '(' and every unmatched '(' at the end needs a ')'.
approach: Keep open = 0 and needed = 0
On '(', increment open
On ')', decrement open if positive, else increment needed
Return open + needed
gotcha: Never let the open counter go negative; an extra ')' must be recorded separately rather than subtracted.

trigger: Count subarrays whose sum equals a target, in an array where sliding-window shrink is awkward (goal may be 0).
key_idea: A subarray [j+1..i] sums to goal iff prefix[i] - prefix[j] == goal, so count how many earlier prefixes equal prefix[i] - goal.
approach: Track running sum and a map of prefix sum counts
For each element, add it to the running sum
If running sum == goal, increment count
Add map[runningSum - goal] to count
Increment map[runningSum]; return count
gotcha: goal == 0 breaks the naive sliding window; the prefix-sum map handles it uniformly (or use atMost(goal) - atMost(goal-1)).

trigger: Construct a permutation with no arithmetic-progression triple nums[i], nums[k], nums[j].
key_idea: Odd + even is never divisible by 2, so put all odds before all evens; a beautiful array A maps to beautiful arrays 2A-1 (odds) and 2A (evens), so build recursively from [1].
approach: Base case n = 1 returns [1]
Recursively build beautiful array for (n+1)//2 and for n//2
Map the first to 2x-1 and the second to 2x
Concatenate odds then evens
Memoize results by n
gotcha: The odd half must use ceil(n/2) elements and the even half floor(n/2), otherwise the result is not a permutation of 1..n.

trigger: Sum of BST node values within [low, high].
key_idea: Use the BST ordering to prune: if a node is below low, only its right subtree can contain valid values; if above high, only the left.
approach: Return 0 for an empty node
If node.val < low, recurse only right
If node.val > high, recurse only left
Otherwise add node.val and recurse both sides
Return the sum

complexity.time: O(n) worst, O(h + k) with pruning

gotcha: Range is inclusive, so use strict < low and > high for the pruning checks.

trigger: Count distinct subsequences of a string modulo 10^9+7.
key_idea: Appending char c to every existing subsequence (plus the empty one) doubles the count, but subsequences that ended in c previously were already counted, so subtract the count contributed the last time c was seen.
approach: Keep total = 0 and last[c] = subsequences ending in c
For each char c, new = total + 1 - last[c]
total = (total + new) mod M
last[c] += new
Return total mod M
gotcha: Subtracting can go negative before the modulo in some languages; in Python the final % M fixes it, elsewhere add M first.

trigger: Make all values unique using only +1 increments, minimizing total increments.
key_idea: Duplicates at value v must push up to v+1, cascading; a counting array (or a sorted sweep) lets you carry the surplus forward and charge one move per carried element.
approach: Build a count array sized len(nums) + max(nums)
Sweep i from 0 upward
If count[i] > 1, carry dup = count[i] - 1 to count[i+1]
Add dup to the total moves
Return the total
gotcha: The count array needs headroom of len(nums) beyond the max value because all duplicates can cascade past it.
